terms: Iconology revisited
W J T Mitchell's Picture Theory 1994; pictorial turn; image as agent rather than passive sign.
Kress and van Leeuwen
Reading Images 1996 grammar of visual design; represented and interactive meanings; vectors, gaze, framing.
Peirce's triadic sign
Charles Sanders Peirce (1839-1914); icon (resemblance), index (causal), symbol (convention); applied to photography by Rosalind Krauss 1977.
Roland Barthes
Rhetoric of the Image 1964 analysed Panzani ad; denotation vs connotation; Mythologies 1957 popularised semiotic critique.
Saussurean sign
Course in General Linguistics 1916; signifier and signified arbitrarily linked; basis for semiotic analysis of image.
Visual rhetoric
Gillian Rose's Visual Methodologies 2001 systematised four sites (production, image, audiencing, circulation) and three modalities.
Comparative study (CS)
IBDP Visual Arts external assessment; 10-15 screens (HL) analysing at least 3 artworks by different artists from different cultural contexts.
Contextual analysis
Situates artwork in historical, social, religious or political context; Erwin Panofsky's iconology three-tier method (Studies in Iconology 1939).
Cross-cultural comparison
Sets artworks from distinct cultures in dialogue; CS rubric requires at least two cultural contexts including a non-Western tradition.
Formal analysis
Examination of line, shape, colour, texture, space and composition; influenced by Heinrich Wolfflin's Principles of Art History 1915.
Function and purpose
Considers ritual, devotional, political, commercial uses; Alfred Gell's Art and Agency 1998 examines artworks as social agents.
Iconography vs iconology
Iconography identifies motifs and conventions; iconology interprets meaning within worldview; Panofsky distinguished them in 1939.
Curatorial rationale
Up to 700-word written statement explaining intent, themes, choices of presentation and connections among works.
Documenta and biennale model
Documenta Kassel founded 1955 by Arnold Bode; Venice Biennale since 1895; established global curatorial benchmarks.
IBDP exhibition
Visual Arts internal assessment; HL submits 8-11 resolved artworks; SL 4-7; coherent presentation in physical or virtual space.
Salon hang vs minimalist hang
Salon densely stacks works floor-to-ceiling (Paris Salon 1737); minimalist isolates each piece at eye-line for sustained contemplation.
Site-specific curation
Robert Smithson's 1968 Site/Non-site; works responsive to architectural and social context (e.g. Olafur Eliasson Weather Project Tate 2003).
White cube model
Brian O'Doherty's Inside the White Cube 1976 critiques the neutral gallery; standard since MoMA's 1930s Alfred Barr installations.
Art-making forms requirement
HL must show sustained experimentation in at least three forms from two columns: 2D, 3D, lens-based, digital.
Critical investigation
Reflective evaluation drawing on art historical influences (e.g. Cy Twombly's mark-making, Yayoi Kusama's infinity nets) to inform practice.
Documentation of process
Annotated photographs, video stills, contact sheets, swatches; records experiments, including unsuccessful ones for critical analysis.
Process portfolio
IBDP Visual Arts external assessment; 9-18 screens (HL) documenting experimentation across art-making forms and media.
Skill acquisition
Documented mastery of techniques (etching, glazing, raku firing, motion capture) through annotated trials and iterative refinement.
Visual journal
Sketchbook of ongoing investigation; tracks artists studied, media tested, contextual research and self-evaluation; not directly assessed but underpins PP.
Artist's context
An artist's training, beliefs and circumstances, which inform how their work can be interpreted.
Audience
Who the work was made for; intended viewers influence its content, materials and manner of display.
Comparison across cultures
Examining artworks from different times and places to reveal similarities, differences and influences.
Conventions
Accepted ways of representing subjects within a tradition, including materials, symbols, formats and styles.
Cultural context
The beliefs, values and conditions of the society in which an artwork was made, which shape its form and meaning.
Function and purpose
Why an artwork was made — devotional, commemorative, political, decorative or commercial roles all shape its form.
